claim_text: Todoist says an attacker got into its production systems and took some customer information
summary: Todoist says: 'On November 23, 2026, an attacker gained unauthorized access to Todoist's production systems and retrieved some customer information.'
detail: It says it began investigating at 17:01 UTC on Nov 23 after its security monitoring flagged an unexpected administrator account, and that it has since blocked the access paths used in the attack.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Todoist's own notice states it; Privacy Affairs reports the same from the notice.

claim_text: The attacker used a stolen credential for Todoist's code system and then took over an employee's work account
summary: Todoist says that between Nov 22 and 23 an attacker used a stolen credential for its version control system to change automated workflows and get more credentials, then took over an employee's work account to reach its cloud systems.
detail: It says the attacker could also read its source code, but its investigation found no changes to application code.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Todoist's notice describes the route in and gives the times.

claim_text: How the attacker first got the stolen credential is not known
summary: Todoist says it has not established how the attacker first obtained the credential. Its leading theory is that an employee's device may have been compromised, but it says this is unconfirmed.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: The notice says so in its own words.

claim_text: No group has claimed the attack in anything we read
summary: Todoist calls the intruder only 'an attacker'. Neither its notice nor the Privacy Affairs report names anyone or mentions a claim of responsibility or a ransom demand.
detail: We did not open leak or dark-web sites.
label: Not established

claim_text: Email addresses and old password hashes of about 6% of Todoist users were downloaded
summary: Todoist says the attacker downloaded records for about 6% of its users whose passwords were still stored with an older method (salted SHA1): their email addresses, password hashes and account creation dates.
detail: A hash is not the password itself, but Todoist says older hashes 'can be vulnerable to password guessing'. These were accounts whose password had not been changed since Todoist stopped using that method more than a decade ago; it says it should have retired it sooner and has now done so.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Todoist's notice lists the data and the share of users; Privacy Affairs reports the same.

claim_text: For much smaller groups of users, tokens, task text and Outlook email previews were taken
summary: Todoist says the attacker took API and Slack tokens from about 0.003% of users, searched task and comment text of about 0.001% for passwords and keys, and read email previews in connected Outlook mailboxes of about 0.001%.
detail: For the Outlook group it says the requests covered subjects, senders, the first 255 characters of messages and attachment names, not full message bodies. For some token holders the attacker also read project, task and comment data. Todoist says it cannot be certain what the attacker saw, so it is reporting everything that was requested.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Todoist's notice describes each group and its share of users.

claim_text: Todoist says it found no sign the attacker signed in to the accounts whose hashes were taken
summary: Todoist says its review of new sign-in sessions for the 6% group 'found no indication that the attacker signed in to those accounts', and that Google and Apple account passwords were not affected.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The company's own statement. No one outside Todoist has checked it, so Reported.

claim_text: How many accounts were affected is not known
summary: Todoist gives only shares of its users (about 6%, 0.003% and 0.001%), not a number of accounts. Privacy Affairs says Todoist has not said how many accounts the 6% stands for.
label: Not established

claim_text: Todoist disabled affected passwords and tokens, switched off its Outlook add-in and emailed affected users
summary: Todoist says it disabled affected passwords, revoked API tokens, disconnected connected apps and ended sessions. It disabled its Outlook add-in on Nov 24 and finished emailing affected customers on Nov 25.
detail: It also says it revoked and replaced exposed internal credentials and finished revoking affected Slack integration tokens on Nov 25. On Nov 26 (18:02 UTC) it says it emailed customers whose passwords were reset as a precaution, adding: "Their accounts were not compromised."
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Todoist's notice lists the steps with their times.

claim_text: Todoist says users who did not get an email need do nothing
summary: Todoist says affected users should follow its email, reset a disabled password, change it anywhere it was reused and replace keys stored in tasks. 'If you didn't receive an email, there is nothing to do.'
detail: It warns users to watch for fake emails about the incident.
label: Reported

claim_text: Whether regulators or police have been told is not known
summary: Todoist's notice does not mention regulators or law enforcement. Privacy Affairs says it has asked Todoist whether regulators have been told; its report shows no answer.
label: Not established
